Europe, through its ciphered letters.

From diplomatic letters to telegrams: recover the texts, understand their stakes and show how they can be read.

This journal opens with two letters from Marie de’ Medici to her ambassador in Rome. The images, proposed readings and uncertainties can be examined together.

1825

Madrid · Everett · Zea Bermúdez

What Everett would not write in clear

Spain will never recognise its former colonies, Zea tells the United States minister. In cipher, Everett writes that he does not believe it: a language imposed by the rival party and by Russia. A passage cut from the 1826 printing, and eight pages never printed.

1675

Copenhagen · Griffenfeld · Louis XIV

The price of Danish neutrality

In the spring of 1675 Denmark promises war to the allies at The Hague and secretly bargains over its neutrality with France: 600,000 écus, then 300,000 a year, an engagement handed to Terlon on 11 June and a Swedish marriage to please Louis XIV. Three months later the Scanian War begins.

1663

Afonso VI · Count of Vila Flor

1663 · Lisbon → the Alentejo army

“Even exposing yourself to the last extremity of a battle.” On 15 May 1663, the day after Don John of Austria invested Évora, Afonso VI ordered the Count of Vila Flor, in cipher, to risk everything to relieve the city. On 26 May, with Évora fallen, the order was repeated. On 8 June came Ameixial. Four ciphered letters, of 13, 15 and 26 May, are read in the record.

1593

Duplessis-Mornay · Tours

1593 · “the king is betrayed”

In 1824 the editors of Duplessis-Mornay's correspondence printed eight cipher passages from two letters of the summer of 1593 as they stood: they had no key. Two centuries later, the “folded” alphabet can be read. At Tours, while the League looks for a king and Henri IV abjures at Saint-Denis, the Protestant leader's correspondents put in cipher what they dare not write in clear: a decree planned to have the Duke of Guise quartered, packets stolen by the Duchess of Angoulême's people, the Count of Gramont in a plot in Béarn, the chancellor and Sourdis behind the truce — “le roy est trahi”, the king is betrayed. Starting hypothesis (“two letters per group”): Daniel Bourdeau (catalogue no. 371).

1675

Copenhagen · Just Høeg

1675 · Copenhagen → The Hague — the Elector wavers

January 1675: the Swedish army has just entered Brandenburg. In Copenhagen, Conrad Biermann, secretary of the German Chancery, copies every week the dispatches leaving for The Hague and Paris; their sensitive passages are in cipher. Thanks to an untitled key sheet in the “Chiffer” volume of the Rigsarkivet, they can be read again: Denmark watches, anxious, as the Elector of Brandenburg wavers — a few months before entering the war against Sweden itself (September 1675, the Scanian War). Thirty-seven letters, January–June 1675, to Høeg and to Meyercrone, read in full: the first published decipherment, to our knowledge.

1710

Charles XII · Bender

1710 · Charles XII, Bender — a “free hand” for an armistice

Bender, 26 April 1710. In exile among the Ottomans, Charles XII — reputed to be closed to any peace — writes in cipher that he is willing to negotiate with Denmark under Anglo-Dutch mediation, and gives the Council a “free hand” for an armistice, “even for a whole year”. Two enciphered copies, forgotten at Stade, read with a reconstructed key.

1532

Ferducci · Fiume

1532 · Ferducci, Fiume — “we shall pretend to go fishing”

Eight enciphered words in a letter otherwise in clear. On 19 July 1532, as Süleyman marched on Vienna, Ferdinand I's agent at Fiume offered to seize the French ambassador at sea on his way back from the sultan — most probably Antonio Rincon. A new reading of an unglossed letter, with a key drawn from contemporary decipherments and confirmed by an independent table of 1542.

1593

Rome · Legate Filippo Sega

Rome’s instruction to the legate, 14 May 1593

Twelve pages of continuous figures: excommunication, a third party, the Infanta’s claim against the Salic law, fear of Navarre’s “feigned conversion”. A probable and partial decipherment; earlier preliminary reading by Satoshi Tomokiyo (2019).

Our method →

01 · The document

Start from the signs

Facsimiles and archive references accompany the transcriptions. A graphical resemblance remains a decision to explain.

02 · The reading

Keep the layers distinct

The image, transcribed sign, proposed value and modernised text are separate. Contextual restorations remain visible.

03 · The evidence

Retain the reservations

A coherent sentence does not prove a key. Unresolved points, corrections and earlier work belong in the dossier.
